cues.text: I stand at the edge of the thin ice of the soul, under which the ocean rages, flakes and cries.
My red hair bleaches with every second, it feels like a little more – and the blue of loneliness will
glint in it. I fall to pieces looking at you, little blue ball, my little grief, love from the
distant planet Solaris – there are so many high temperatures and radio waves inside you – I don’t
think I’ll stand this much love and this much vastness if I keep staring at the horizon for even one
more minute – and the sand dries my feet out so, chills them so – I don’t think I’ll stand this much
aging and this much loneliness, knowing that all your gigantic mother-of-pearl warmth and all the
love in the world are right here before me – but I can’t drown in you.
And that’s not even it – I still choose to stick to the shore and know that it, that very thing – is
only on the horizon of a toy world, close to a glitch in the matrix.
Your limits are out of my reach. I can see it keenly.
At some point I grew so fused with the thought of my own motherhood and estrangement at the sight of
you that my body started to deform. Every day I cry the bitterest and quietest tears to moisten the
air with you and make it a little more like your saltiness.
I cry to exhaustion, cry for you, cry so I won’t forget what you taste like, so my heels on the bare
beach won’t turn completely to ice, I cry – fall into the sand from exhaustion and cold mixed with
blood – wake to the smell of sweat and grief – hug my knees and belly – cry again.
One day I cried so much that the next morning I woke with a new outgrowth: my belly had gone round
and glassy, like half a fishbowl. A plastic snorkel ran from it straight to my chapped lips.
I felt an unbelievable thirst that day – and, gulping down water from the fishbowl tube, I felt my
veins fill again with your salty lymph and microalgae – and I lapped it up for hours until I had the
strength to cry again. Since then I’ve been a landbound scuba diver.
Every day I look at my big unwieldy belly and feel disgust.
I hate this outgrowth, I’m so ashamed to admit it’s part of me that sometimes I throw up right onto
the beach sand. It reminds me how I die of thirst without you.
It reminds me that you exist and that I’ll never be able to leave this beach, because there’s no such
thing as scuba divers without oceans. Even landbound ones.
I despise my watery belly with all my guts, but I don’t dare smash it.
I know your liquid is seething in the depths of my belly, the liquid you put in me out of love for
me. I know: even if one morning I don’t wake up to mourn you again, my microcosm will breathe for me
through the thin little scuba tube. Unless it stops being enough for me, and I drink every last drop.
I stand at the edge of the thin ice of the soul that I, we, he and they so fragilely, so carelessly –
I stand there and slurp the last of my strength through a cocktail straw.
